_about: Hand-written descriptions for joints, ligaments, intervertebral discs and costal cartilages without a Wikipedia text. See app/extra_content.py.

Articular capsule of acromioclavicular j.description:
Thin fibrous capsule enclosing the plane synovial joint between the lateral end of the clavicle and the acromion, thickened above as the acromioclavicular ligament. It gives horizontal stability, while vertical stability comes mainly from the coracoclavicular (conoid and trapezoid) ligaments.
A fall on the point of the shoulder tears the capsule first (grade I-II separation) and then the coracoclavicular ligaments, letting the clavicle ride up (step deformity).

Articular capsule of sternoclavicular jo.description:
Strong fibrous capsule of the saddle-shaped synovial joint between the medial clavicle, the clavicular notch of the manubrium and the first costal cartilage. Reinforced by the anterior and posterior sternoclavicular, interclavicular and costoclavicular ligaments, and divided by an articular disc, it is so strong that the clavicle usually fractures before the joint dislocates.
This is the only bony joint between the upper limb and the axial skeleton; posterior dislocation can compress the great vessels and trachea.

Articular capsule of superior tibiofibul.description: Fibrous capsule of the plane synovial joint between the head of the fibula and the lateral condyle of the tibia, reinforced by anterior and posterior ligaments of the fibular head. The joint allows slight gliding as the fibula rotates during ankle movement; its cavity communicates with the knee joint in about 10% of people.

Articular capsule of interphalangeal joi.description: Fibrous capsule of the single hinge joint of the hallux, strengthened by collateral ligaments at the sides and a plantar plate below. Flexion is produced by flexor hallucis longus and extension by extensor hallucis longus.

Articular capsules of distal interphalan.description:
Fibrous capsules of the hinge joints between the middle and distal phalanges of the fingers, reinforced by collateral ligaments and a palmar plate. Flexion is by flexor digitorum profundus alone.
They are the site of Heberden nodes in osteoarthritis; rupture of the extensor tendon at its insertion here causes a mallet finger.

Articular capsules of proximal interphal.description:
Fibrous capsules of the hinge joints between the proximal and middle phalanges of the fingers, reinforced by strong collateral ligaments and a thick palmar plate that prevents hyperextension. Flexion is by flexor digitorum superficialis (and profundus).
They are the site of Bouchard nodes in osteoarthritis, are commonly involved in rheumatoid arthritis, and are often injured (dorsal dislocation, volar plate injury) in ball sports.

Articular capsules of distal interphalan.description: Fibrous capsules of the hinge joints between the middle and distal phalanges of the lesser toes, reinforced by collateral ligaments and plantar plates. Flexion is by flexor digitorum longus. Fixed flexion here produces a mallet toe.

Articular capsules of proximal interphal.description: Fibrous capsules of the hinge joints between the proximal and middle phalanges of the lesser toes, with collateral ligaments and plantar plates. Fixed flexion of these joints with extension at the metatarsophalangeal joint gives a hammer toe.

Articular capsules of metatarsophalangea.description:
Fibrous capsules of the condyloid joints between the metatarsal heads and the proximal phalanges, reinforced by collateral ligaments and a thick plantar plate linked by the deep transverse metatarsal ligaments. They allow flexion, extension and a little abduction and adduction, and take high loads during toe-off.
The first MTP joint is the classic site of gout (podagra) and of hallux valgus and hallux rigidus.

Capitohamate interosseous ligament.description: Strong intrinsic ligament joining the adjacent surfaces of the capitate and hamate within the distal carpal row. The distal row moves as a nearly rigid unit with the metacarpals, and these interosseous ligaments bind it together.

Palmar capitohamate ligament.description: Short intrinsic ligament crossing the palmar surface of the capitate-hamate joint, helping to bind the distal carpal row into a stable unit.

Trapeziotrapezoidal interosseous ligamen.description: Intrinsic interosseous ligament joining the trapezium and trapezoid within the distal carpal row.

Trapezoideocapitate interosseous ligamen.description: Intrinsic interosseous ligament joining the trapezoid and capitate within the distal carpal row.

Palmar trapezoideocapitate ligament.description: Short intrinsic ligament on the palmar surface of the joint between the trapezoid and capitate, binding the distal carpal row.

Scapholunate interosseous ligament.description:
C-shaped intrinsic ligament joining the proximal edges of the scaphoid and lunate, with a thick dorsal part that is its strongest component, a proximal membranous part and a palmar part. It is the key stabiliser of the proximal carpal row.
Its tear (after a fall on the outstretched hand) lets the scaphoid flex and the lunate extend, widening the scapholunate gap on X-ray (Terry Thomas sign) and leading to DISI instability and eventually SLAC arthritis.

Lunotriquetral interosseous ligament.description: C-shaped intrinsic ligament joining the lunate and triquetrum in the proximal carpal row, strongest palmarly. Its tear produces ulnar-sided wrist pain and, with further ligament damage, a VISI (volar flexed lunate) instability pattern.

Palmar lunotriquetral ligament.description: Palmar thickening of the lunotriquetral ligament complex, joining the palmar surfaces of the lunate and triquetrum; it is the strongest part of the lunotriquetral linkage.

Dorsal scaphotriquetral ligament.description: Dorsal intercarpal ligament running from the triquetrum across the back of the lunate to the scaphoid (and trapezium). With the dorsal radiocarpal ligament it forms a lateral V that stabilises the proximal row and is a secondary stabiliser of the scapholunate joint.

Palmar scaphotriquetral ligament.description: Palmar intercarpal ligament arching from the triquetrum to the scaphoid across the palmar surface of the carpus, supporting the head of the capitate. Together with the other palmar arcuate ligaments it forms the distal limb of the palmar V.

Radiocapitate ligament.description: Palmar extrinsic ligament running from the radial styloid across the waist of the scaphoid, which rests in it like a sling, to the capitate. It stabilises the scaphoid and helps prevent ulnar translation of the carpus. The space of Poirier, a weak area between it and the long radiolunate ligament, is where perilunate dislocations tear through.

Scaphocapitate ligament.description: Palmar intrinsic ligament from the distal pole of the scaphoid to the capitate, supporting the distal scaphoid and linking the two carpal rows.

Scaphotrapeziotrapezoidal ligament.description: Ligament complex around the STT joint between the distal pole of the scaphoid and the trapezium and trapezoid. It stabilises the distal scaphoid; osteoarthritis of the STT joint is a common source of radial-sided wrist pain, often coexisting with thumb base arthritis.

Triquetrocapitate ligament.description: Palmar intrinsic ligament from the triquetrum to the capitate, forming the ulnar limb of the palmar arcuate ligament. It stabilises the midcarpal joint; its laxity contributes to midcarpal instability (a painful clunk on ulnar deviation).

Triquetrohamate ligament.description: Palmar intrinsic ligament from the triquetrum to the hamate, part of the ulnar arm of the palmar arcuate ligament that stabilises the midcarpal joint.

Pisotriquetral ligament.description: Ligament binding the pisiform to the palmar surface of the triquetrum around the small pisotriquetral synovial joint. The pisiform is a sesamoid bone in the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris, whose pull continues distally as the pisohamate and pisometacarpal ligaments.

Cuneocuboid interosseous ligament.description: Strong interosseous ligament binding the lateral cuneiform to the cuboid, part of the ligament system that holds the transverse arch of the midfoot.

Intercuneiform interosseous ligaments.description: Strong interosseous ligaments binding the medial, intermediate and lateral cuneiforms together, keeping the wedge-shaped bones locked into the transverse arch of the foot.

Cuneometatarsal interosseous ligaments.description: Interosseous ligaments binding the cuneiforms to the bases of the metatarsals at the tarsometatarsal (Lisfranc) joints. The most important runs from the medial cuneiform to the base of the second metatarsal (the Lisfranc ligament); its rupture destabilises the midfoot and is easily missed on non-weight-bearing radiographs.

Talocalcaneal interosseous ligament.description: Strong, broad ligament in the tarsal sinus and canal, joining the sulcus tali to the calcaneal sulcus between the posterior subtalar joint and the talocalcaneonavicular joint. It is the main bond between talus and calcaneus and resists eversion; the sinus tarsi can become painful after inversion injuries.

Posterior tibiotalar ligament.description: Deepest and strongest posterior part of the deltoid (medial collateral) ligament of the ankle, running from the medial malleolus to the medial side and medial tubercle of the talus. It resists eversion and external rotation of the talus; the deltoid ligament is so strong that eversion injuries often avulse the medial malleolus instead of tearing it.

Anterior meniscotibial ligament (Lateral.description: Fibrous root attaching the anterior horn of the lateral meniscus to the intercondylar area of the tibia, in front of the lateral intercondylar tubercle and close to the ACL. Intact meniscal roots are essential for the meniscus to convert axial load into hoop stress; a root tear is functionally equivalent to a total meniscectomy.

Posterior meniscotibial ligament (Latera.description: Fibrous root attaching the posterior horn of the lateral meniscus to the tibia behind the lateral intercondylar tubercle. Posterior lateral root tears are commonly associated with ACL ruptures.

Anterior meniscotibial ligament (Medial.description: Fibrous root anchoring the anterior horn of the medial meniscus to the front of the anterior intercondylar area of the tibia, in front of the ACL attachment.

Posterior meniscotibial ligament (Medial.description: Fibrous root anchoring the posterior horn of the medial meniscus to the posterior intercondylar area of the tibia, in front of the PCL. Degenerative posterior root tears are common in middle-aged and older people and lead to meniscal extrusion and rapid medial compartment arthritis.

Frenula capsulae.description: Frenula of the capsule (retinacula) of the hip joint: synovial folds on the femoral neck, formed where capsular fibres are reflected back along the neck. They carry the retinacular branches of the circumflex femoral arteries to the femoral head.

Descending part of iliofemoral ligament.description: The medial (inferior) band of the Y-shaped iliofemoral ligament, running from the anterior inferior iliac spine to the lower part of the intertrochanteric line. The iliofemoral ligament is the strongest ligament of the body; it tightens in extension so that the upright body can rest on it with little muscle effort, and resists hyperextension.

Inferior transverse scapular ligament.description: The spinoglenoid ligament: a thin band bridging the spinoglenoid notch between the lateral border of the scapular spine and the glenoid margin. The suprascapular nerve and vessels pass under it to the infraspinous fossa; a ganglion cyst here can compress the nerve and cause isolated infraspinatus weakness.

Sacrococcygeal symphysis.description: Cartilaginous joint between the apex of the sacrum and the base of the coccyx, with a thin fibrocartilaginous disc and anterior, posterior and lateral sacrococcygeal ligaments. It allows the coccyx to move back slightly during defaecation and childbirth; injury from a fall on the buttocks causes coccydynia. It often fuses with age.

Nucleus pulposus C2-C3.description:
Gelatinous core of the intervertebral disc between the C2 and C3 vertebrae, a remnant of the notochord. It is rich in proteoglycans and water, which let it resist compression and spread load evenly onto the surrounding anulus fibrosus and the vertebral end plates; it loses water and height with age.
A posterolateral herniation compresses the nerve root at the corresponding foramen; a large central herniation can compress the spinal cord (cervical) or cauda equina (lumbar).

Costal cartilage of first rib.description:
Short, broad bar of hyaline cartilage joining the first rib to the manubrium at a primary cartilaginous joint (synchondrosis), which allows almost no movement. It often ossifies early in adult life.
Inflammation at the costochondral and sternocostal junctions (costochondritis) is a common cause of chest-wall pain.

Costal cartilage of second rib.description:
Bar of hyaline cartilage continuing the second rib forward to the sternum at a synovial sternocostal joint. Costal cartilages give the chest wall its elasticity during breathing and cushion blows to the thorax; they calcify with age, which can be seen on chest radiographs.
The second cartilage meets the sternum at the sternal angle (of Louis), the landmark for counting ribs.
Inflammation at the costochondral and sternocostal junctions (costochondritis) is a common cause of chest-wall pain.

The seventh is the last and longest cartilage to reach the sternum, near the xiphisternal junction.
Inflammation at the costochondral and sternocostal junctions (costochondritis) is a common cause of chest-wall pain.

Costal cartilage of eighth rib.description:
Bar of hyaline cartilage continuing the eighth rib forward. As a false rib it does not reach the sternum but joins the cartilage above, forming part of the costal margin (arch) that bounds the infrasternal angle.
Inflammation at the costochondral and sternocostal junctions (costochondritis) is a common cause of chest-wall pain.

Costal cartilage of tenth rib.description:

As a false rib it does not reach the sternum but joins the cartilage above, forming part of the costal margin (arch) that bounds the infrasternal angle. The tenth costal cartilage marks the lowest point of the costal margin, at about the level of L3.
Inflammation at the costochondral and sternocostal junctions (costochondritis) is a common cause of chest-wall pain.
